terms.definition: An IAM advanced feature that sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant to a user or role. It is a positive construct listing allowed actions — it never grants anything by itself.
terms.example: Like a hotel key card that only works on floors 1-3, no matter which master key the admin gives you.

terms.definition: A policy passed as a parameter at the moment you call STS:AssumeRole. It applies only to that one session and can only narrow permissions — never widen them beyond what the role already allows.
terms.example: Like a day-pass at a theme park that lets you into the park but restricts you to certain rides, even if your season pass covers everything.

terms.definition: The AWS service that issues temporary security credentials (access key ID, secret access key, session token) when a principal assumes an IAM role. Credentials expire when the session ends.
terms.example: Like a visitor badge system — you request access, get a time-limited badge, do your work, and the badge expires automatically.

terms.definition: The STS API call that allows a principal to take on an IAM role and receive temporary credentials. Requires STS:AssumeRole permission on the caller side and a trust policy on the role side.
terms.example: Like borrowing a colleague's access card for the day — you temporarily get their permissions, then return the card.

terms.definition: A resource-based policy attached to an IAM role that defines which principals are allowed to assume the role. It answers the question: 'Who is allowed to wear this costume?'
terms.example: Like a backstage pass list — only the names on the list can come backstage.

terms.definition: A security vulnerability in cross-account access where a third-party service (like a SaaS vendor) is tricked into accessing one customer's resources while acting on behalf of a different customer.
terms.example: Like a locksmith being told 'open this door' by someone pretending to be the owner — the locksmith (deputy) gets confused about who they're actually serving.

terms.definition: A unique identifier added as a condition in a role's trust policy, used to prevent the Confused Deputy problem. The assuming party must pass this value on every AssumeRole call.
terms.example: Like a secret code word that only the real client knows — a different client can't guess it.

terms.definition: The pattern where a principal in one AWS account accesses resources in a different AWS account, typically via role assumption using STS. Requires a two-policy handshake.
terms.example: Like a contractor from Company B getting a guest badge at Company A's office to do a specific job, then leaving.

terms.definition: The requirement for cross-account role assumption: (1) the caller in the source account needs STS:AssumeRole permission, AND (2) the role in the destination account needs a trust policy naming the caller. Both are required.
terms.example: Like two locks on a safe — both must be unlocked for the door to open.

terms.definition: In cross-account access, the account where the calling principal (e.g., EC2 instance) originates. This is where the STS:AssumeRole permission must exist. Often confused with the destination.
terms.example: If EC2 in Account B accesses S3 in Account A, Account B is the source — it's where the call originates.

terms.definition: In cross-account access, the account that holds the resource being accessed and the role being assumed. The role's trust policy, bucket policy, and KMS key policy all live here.
terms.example: Account A (the one with S3 and KMS) is the destination — it's where the role and data are.

terms.definition: An IAM policy attached directly to a principal (user, group, or role). It answers 'what can this identity do?' The Principal element is implicit because the policy is attached to that identity.
terms.example: Like a job description — it defines what the employee (identity) is allowed to do.

terms.definition: A policy attached to an AWS resource (S3 bucket, KMS key, Lambda, etc.) that defines who can access it. The Principal element must be explicit. Supports cross-account access without role assumption.
terms.example: Like a building's access control list — the building itself decides who can enter, regardless of the visitor's own credentials.

terms.definition: A Deny statement in any IAM policy that overrides every Allow — in any policy type, same account or cross-account. The first rule of IAM evaluation: explicit deny wins, always.
terms.example: Like a blacklist — if you're on it, no VIP pass or invitation overrides it.

terms.definition: The default state in AWS: if no explicit Allow exists for an action, it is denied. AWS is deny-by-default — the absence of a permission means no permission.
terms.example: Like a locked door — not being on the allowed list doesn't mean you're explicitly banned, but you still can't get in.

terms.definition: A container that associates an IAM role with an EC2 instance. The EC2 instance uses the instance profile to assume the role automatically, providing temporary credentials without storing access keys.
terms.example: Like a company laptop that automatically logs into company systems when you turn it on — no manual login needed.

terms.definition: An IAM condition key (boolean) that returns true if the session was authenticated with MFA at any point during its lifetime. It stays true for the entire session — even hours after MFA was performed.
terms.example: Like an all-day wristband at an event — once you get it, it's valid for the whole day.

terms.definition: An IAM condition key (numeric, in seconds) that measures how long ago MFA was performed. Used with NumericLessThan to enforce fresh MFA for sensitive operations. Defends against session hijacking.
terms.example: Like a parking ticket — it shows how long you've been parked. If it exceeds the limit, you can't access certain areas.

terms.definition: When accessing KMS-encrypted resources cross-account, BOTH the IAM role's permission policy AND the KMS key's resource policy must independently permit KMS:Decrypt. Missing either one causes Access Denied.
terms.example: Like a two-person rule for a bank vault — both the manager and the clerk must authorize, independently.

terms.definition: A hardware-based MFA device using public key cryptography (e.g., Google Titan, YubiKey). It is phishing-resistant because the credential is bound to the original domain and cannot be replayed on a different site.
terms.example: Like a physical building key that only works on one specific lock — even if someone copies the key, it won't open another building's door.

terms.definition: An IAM role attached to a Lambda function that defines what the function is allowed to do (e.g., read S3, write to DynamoDB). Separate from who can invoke the Lambda — that's the resource-based policy.
terms.example: Like a stagehand's job description — it defines what they can do backstage, not who hired them.

terms.definition: A predefined IAM role created automatically by an AWS managed service (like ECS, Auto Scaling) with the exact permissions needed for that service. You cannot modify the trust policy or permission scope.
terms.example: Like a contractor with a fixed skillset provided by a staffing agency — you get them as-is, no customization.
